solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: see 26ac.
Land of Bush senior: a major power no more

parts.note: George Bush was President of the United States
Sr is the standard abbreviation for senior

explanation.surface: A dig at the United States under the elder Bush, pictured as a superpower already in decline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush senior' looks like one man, George H. W. Bush; split it, so his country and the abbreviation for senior join up.
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet Union was a superpower until it broke up in 1991, so it no longer exists as a state.

clue.text: Hit and piss on a hack

parts.note: both are British slang for beer, especially weak or cheap beer
a hack is a journalist, and ED is short for the newspaper's editor

explanation.surface: Someone thumps a journalist and then urinates on him, a typical tabloid brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piss' looks like a verb; it is a slang noun for beer, and 'on' puts the editor after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To wallop someone is to strike them hard, so walloped is the past tense meaning struck.

clue.text: Vacillating Hague is ditching centre for a "hostess"

indicators.note: something vacillating wavers back and forth, so the letters do not stay in place
to ditch the centre is to throw away the middle letter of the words in question

parts.note: taken as written; William Hague was a Conservative politician

explanation.surface: A wavering William Hague gives up the centre ground in search of a hostess.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle letter of the seven, the U, goes before the remaining six are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A geisha is a Japanese woman trained to entertain male guests, so a hostess in quotation marks hints at that role.

clue.text: see 19ac.
Remarked about "rubbish" Cable, ultimately a burden on the Treasury

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for remarked goes round the rest
ultimately points to the last letter of the name it follows

parts.note: the last letter of Cable; Vince Cable was Business Secretary

explanation.surface: A jibe at Vince Cable, said to be rubbish and a drain on public money.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb for remarked is split around the junk and the final letter of the politician's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Government subsidy to industry is paid from public funds, so it weighs on the Treasury's budget.

clue.text: Man's screwed in the country show

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the country's abbreviation
something screwed up is twisted and mangled out of its order

explanation.surface: A man has sex somewhere out in the countryside, as if at a rural fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the country show' reads as an agricultural event; the definition is only the last word, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To unmask is to reveal or expose, which is what 'show' means as a verb here.

clue.text: Swots then craps, perhaps — a thankless task

parts.note: to mug up is to swot, so mugs means swots
craps is a dice game, and perhaps marks it as an example

explanation.surface: A student cramming then gambling at dice has picked a pointless pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craps' looks like vulgar slang, but it is the dice game.
explanation.definitionFit: A mug's game is an idiom for an activity only a fool would take on, being unrewarding.

clue.text: Frequently lose an erection, going without head?

indicators.note: going without a head means the first letter is lost

parts.note: to lose stiffness is to go soft

explanation.surface: A rude question about how often a man goes limp, perhaps when headless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' has a smutty surface sense; here it is the first letter of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Often and frequently are plain synonyms for something happening many times.

clue.text: Inflamed Brenda snuggles up to gangster, just as it was written

parts.note: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A randy Queen cuddles up to a mobster, a classic Private Eye fantasy.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's name for Queen Elizabeth II, so she stands for her royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal reading or translation keeps exactly to the original words, without interpretation.

clue.text: Clear fortune — not half — taken by cops

indicators.note: not half asks for only half of the word for fortune to be kept

parts.note: the Criminal Investigation Department, the detective branch of British police

explanation.surface: Half of a fortune is seized by the police, leaving the rest clear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not half' is British slang for 'very much', but here it literally halves the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucid means clear in the sense of easily understood or clear-headed.

clue.text: Winsome female "given one" — means nothing

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A charming woman has been 'given one', slang for sex, and it means nothing to her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given one' is British slang for having sex with someone; only 'one' supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet FA, short for sweet Fanny Adams, is British slang for absolutely nothing at all.

clue.text: Nick wants a hack punished

parts.note: a hack is a journalist, and the editor is ED

explanation.surface: A policeman wants a journalist punished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a verb meaning arrest; it is the noun for a prison.
explanation.definitionFit: To be caned is to be beaten with a stick as a punishment, as in old schools.

clue.text: Denies CID's smashed anti-government activities

indicators.note: smashed means broken to pieces, so the letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone denies the detective squad crushed protests against the government.
explanation.definitionFit: Dissidence is open disagreement with or opposition to an established regime.

clue.text: "Plan A — it's crap; left with Nick, finally" — not what you'd expect to hear from Cameron say, publicly?

definitions.text: not what you'd expect to hear from Cameron say, publicly?

indicators.note: something crap is broken and useless, so the letters are rebuilt

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left

indicators.note: finally keeps just the closing letter of the word before it

parts.note: the last letter of Nick; Nick Clegg was Cameron's coalition deputy

explanation.surface: A frank verdict on George Osborne's austerity Plan A, the kind of honesty David Cameron would never voice in public.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue sounds like an aside; the definition is the satirical question, mocking politicians' evasive language.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain talk is frank, straightforward speech, which the clue suggests a spin-minded prime minister avoids.

clue.text: Insult by American: "Miliband's redundant"

explanation.surface: An American insults the Labour leader as surplus to requirements.
explanation.definitionFit: Something disused is no longer in service, so it has become redundant.

clue.text: Excellent old-fashioned sexual activity for some

definitions.meaning: first meaning: splendid, as in a fine thing in tip-top condition
second meaning: slapping the buttocks, a fetish associated with the old school

explanation.surface: Someone enthuses about a traditional kink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old-fashioned' reads as describing the activity; in the first sense the adjective itself is a dated piece of British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanking is an informal adjective for very good or brisk, and also the noun for smacking someone's bottom.

clue.text: Balls trapped in spinning wheel? Do some sweet-talking

indicators.note: trapped in means held inside the other letters
something spinning is whirled round, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: Ed Balls, the Labour shadow chancellor

explanation.surface: A schoolboy joke about testicles caught in a spinning wheel, followed by smooth talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is not anatomy but the politician Ed Balls.
explanation.definitionFit: To wheedle is to coax or persuade someone by flattery, which is to sweet-talk them.

clue.text: Rotate possible cannabis holder; it facilitates inhaling

parts.note: to wind is to turn something round
a pipe may be used for smoking cannabis

explanation.surface: Pass the joint, or rather the pipe, round: it is for inhaling.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic hint at the trachea, the tube that carries air to the lungs.
explanation.definitionFit: The windpipe is the trachea, the air passage from throat to lungs that every breath passes through.

clue.text: Royal favourite: drugs and nooky

explanation.surface: The royals' favourite pastimes are drugs and sex.
explanation.walkthrough: The Earl of Essex was Elizabeth I's favourite courtier; Essex is also an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, was the famous favourite of Queen Elizabeth I until his execution.

clue.text: (& 5dn.) Mixed party rule: Fuel sex with molecular charge control

parts.note: an ion is a charged atom or molecule

explanation.surface: A sex-and-science riff on the Cameron–Clegg pact in power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed party' reads like an orgy; it means a government formed by two parties.
explanation.definitionFit: A coalition government is rule by several parties sharing power, as in Britain in 2010–15.

clue.text: Appendix snipped and wrapped in blubber — naff

indicators.note: wrapped in means placed inside the other word

parts.note: to blubber is to cry noisily

indicators.note: snipped means cut short, so most of the word is chopped off

explanation.surface: An appendectomy, the organ sewn up in fat, sounds like a poor operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blubber' looks like body fat, but it is the verb to weep. Naff is British slang for tacky or rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Crappy and naff are both slang words meaning shoddy, cheap or of poor quality.

clue.text: Location of bodily secretion said to be determined

indicators.note: said tells us to judge the words by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: a cyst is a sac in the body containing fluid

explanation.surface: A medical description of where some fluid is found, stated firmly.
explanation.definitionFit: To insist is to be determined in demanding or asserting something, refusing to give way.

clue.text: X, in a calculating way, shows organ

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the multiplication sign is read aloud as this word
second meaning: a newspaper, here the London daily

explanation.surface: A calculator's X apparently reveals a body part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' looks anatomical but means a newspaper, the mouthpiece of a group.
explanation.definitionFit: In arithmetic X means multiplied by, and The Times is a British newspaper, an organ of the press.

clue.text: Nuts free? Capital!

parts.note: to rid is to free of something

explanation.surface: An exclamation that free nuts are a capital idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital!' looks like an old-fashioned cry of approval; it is the definition, a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Madrid is the capital city of Spain.

clue.text: Ken, last sporting bangles round base of member

indicators.note: sporting can mean frolicking about, so the letters play around

explanation.surface: Ken wears jewellery around the base of his penis, a smutty image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' suggests the penis but means a limb: the leg, whose base is the ankle.
explanation.definitionFit: Anklets are ornamental bands worn around the ankle, which sits at the bottom of the leg, a limb.

clue.text: Absurdity of outspoken airborne troop MOs?

indicators.note: outspoken means spoken out loud, so we go by the sound of the words

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper, and MOs are medical officers, army doctors

explanation.surface: Blunt-speaking regimental doctors in the Parachute Regiment are a strange contradiction.
explanation.walkthrough: MO is Medical Officer, an army doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A paradox is a seemingly self-contradictory statement or situation, something apparently absurd.

clue.text: One into zip undoing

indicators.note: into means going inside the following word

parts.note: to zip is to move fast, run

explanation.surface: Someone is busy unzipping their trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'zip undoing' looks like opening a fly; 'undoing' is the noun for downfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruin and undoing both mean a person's downfall or destruction.

clue.text: (& 1dn.) Put the wind up racing driver, depressed when things get really bad?

definitions.text: depressed when things get really bad?

parts.note: to put the wind up someone is to frighten them, panic them
Jenson Button, Formula One world champion

explanation.surface: A racing driver gets scared, and turns gloomy when things go badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depressed' looks like low spirits; it means pressed down, as an alarm switch is in an emergency.
explanation.definitionFit: A panic button is an alarm switch you push in an emergency, so it is literally pressed down in crisis.

clue.text: A dose of Sly's hip remedy around one

indicators.note: around means surrounding the letter that follows
to remedy something is to put it right, so the letters are fixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone takes a dose of medicine for Sly's bad hip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A dose' looks like a measure of medicine; it is old slang for a venereal infection.
explanation.definitionFit: A dose is slang for a sexually transmitted disease, and syphilis is one such infection.
